caption:
South Korea's education minister Choi Kyo-jin resigned on Sunday after AI cheating fears upended the national college entrance exam.
Phones got emergency alerts mid-exam to expose hidden devices, and 111 test-takers were caught with smart devices.
President Lee Jae Myung accepted his resignation about an hour later.

Should schools ban smart glasses and phones from every exam room?

Follow @neurafeed.ai for daily AI news.

Source: The Korea Herald, Ynet, AP · Photo: Kim Hong-Ji/Pool/Reuters

paragraphs.text: South Korean Education Minister Choi Kyo-jin offered his resignation on Sunday, November 22, 2026, saying he would take responsibility for the confusion caused by last-minute changes meant to stop AI-assisted cheating on the national college entrance exam. According to the presidential office, President Lee Jae Myung accepted the resignation about an hour after it was presented, The Korea Herald reported.

In a statement released by the ministry, Choi said the changes made ahead of the exam had inconvenienced test-takers and the public, and that as minister he could not escape criticism that the ministry had not prepared in advance. Presidential spokesperson Kang Yu-jung said a new minister would be appointed through established procedures, and Lee asked Prime Minister Han Seong-sook to focus on follow-up measures for the exam.
A confession that set off the alarm

The crisis began days before the College Scholastic Ability Test, known as the Suneung, which was held on November 19. According to the Associated Press, Han Won-seok, 34, the top scorer on the national tax accountant exam, admitted in a video posted on November 15 on his lawyer's YouTube channel that he had used a hidden microcamera to capture exam questions, fed the images to a generative AI tool and read the answers on a smartphone. He said he would cooperate with police.

At a National Assembly education committee session on November 16, Choi rejected calls from lawmakers to postpone the college exam, saying a delay would cause a larger disruption for students, the AP reported. He said proctors could spot AI smart glasses with thick horn-rimmed frames. Ynet reported that when he was asked whether authorities could identify every AI-assisted cheater, Choi answered that because of his age he did not think he could. The next day, a former Seoul city council member from the opposition People Power Party filed a police complaint accusing Choi of dereliction of duty.
Emergency alerts in the exam room

On exam day, the government sent three nationwide emergency alerts to phones between 8 a.m. and 3 p.m., according to Ynet. The alerts sounded even on phones set to silent, so any phone hidden in an exam room would ring unless it was fully switched off or in airplane mode. Ynet described it as the first time the national alert system had been used to catch exam cheaters.

Other measures included doubling the number of exam supervisors, blocking public Wi-Fi near exam centers and allowing students to bring only pencils, with erasers provided on site. Students wearing clothes with buttons had to cover them with stickers, and supervisors inspected glasses, watches, collars and sleeves for hidden devices, Ynet reported.

About half a million students took the exam. Officials said 111 test-takers were caught possessing or using smart devices, including one with smart glasses and another with a miniature camera and wireless earphones. Ynet reported that nearly half of the cases were detected through the alerts. The Korea Herald said penalties would be decided before scores are released on December 11.

The government and the ruling Democratic Party have suggested a 10-year exam ban for AI-assisted cheating, possibly applied to this year's test, and authorities are considering a review of past exams, according to The Korea Herald. Lee wrote on X that fairness in examinations is a principle that must never be compromised, Ynet reported.

The episode shows how quickly consumer AI tools have outpaced the way large exams are run. A phone camera and a chatbot were enough to beat a professional licensing test, and the response relied on blunt tools such as national phone alerts and stickers over buttons. Other countries with high-stakes national exams face the same gap between cheap smart devices and exam rules written before them.

The next markers are the penalty decisions for the 111 cases before scores are released on December 11, the choice of a new education minister, and whether the proposed 10-year ban for AI cheating becomes law.
